clinicalPearls: A rare disorder of cortisol metabolism in which regeneration of active cortisol from inactive cortisone is impaired
Caused by defective 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 or, more often in the congenital form, its NADPH-supplying enzyme hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD)
Reduced tissue cortisol regeneration increases cortisol clearance, so the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis compensates by raising ACTH, which drives adrenal androgen output
Presents with androgen excess, including premature pubarche in children, and hirsutism, oligomenorrhoea and a polycystic-ovary-like picture in women
Patients are broadly compensated for cortisol and are not Cushingoid
A characteristic urinary steroid metabolite profile shows a high ratio of cortisone metabolites to cortisol metabolites (tetrahydrocortisone relative to the tetrahydrocortisols)
Management addresses the androgen excess by suppressing ACTH-driven adrenal androgen production with glucocorticoid and using antiandrogen therapy as needed
Should be distinguished from apparent mineralocorticoid excess (an 11-beta-HSD2 defect), which instead causes hypertension
reference.pathophysiology: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 is a predominantly hepatic and adipose enzyme that regenerates active cortisol from inert cortisone, using NADPH generated within the endoplasmic reticulum by hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. In cortisone reductase deficiency, loss-of-function mutations in H6PD, and less commonly in the reductase gene itself, deprive the enzyme of cofactor or directly impair it, so cortisol is not efficiently regenerated and its metabolic clearance rises. To maintain circulating cortisol the pituitary increases ACTH secretion, which secondarily stimulates the adrenal cortex to overproduce androgens. The net clinical effect is androgen excess with a broadly compensated cortisol status rather than frank glucocorticoid deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Non-classic (late-onset) congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Apparent mineralocorticoid excess (11-beta-HSD2 deficiency) as a contrast
additionalInvestigations: 24-hour urinary steroid metabolite profiling by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showing an elevated cortisone-to-cortisol metabolite ratio
Serum androgens including testosterone, androstenedione and DHEAS
Short synacthen or ACTH stimulation to assess adrenal reserve if compensation is in doubt
Molecular genetic testing of H6PD and the 11-beta-HSD1 gene
redFlags: Rapidly progressive virilisation suggesting an androgen-secreting tumour rather than an enzymopathy
Signs of adrenal insufficiency during intercurrent illness if compensation fails
Severe metabolic disturbance in the context of associated obesity and insulin resistance
reference.prognosis: Generally good; androgen-excess features can be managed and, because glucocorticoid status is compensated, patients are usually well, though attention to metabolic health and fertility is worthwhile.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as polycystic ovary syndrome and missing the underlying steroid-metabolism defect on urinary profiling
Confusing it with apparent mineralocorticoid excess (11-beta-HSD2 deficiency), which instead causes hypertension and hypokalaemia
Assuming frank cortisol deficiency and over-treating with glucocorticoid
Overlooking H6PD as the commonest congenital cause when only the reductase gene is tested
references: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism reviews on cortisol metabolism
